key_insight: A submitted solution that closely resembles LLM output does not reliably reveal how much mathematical thinking a student offloaded.
engineering_relevance: Educational AI tools should support process-level evaluation rather than infer student engagement solely from final-answer similarity.
method: Followed 23 first-year linear algebra students using LLMs on three differently designed homework tasks.
Interpreted 429 prompts as traces of self-regulation and compared 59 chatlogs with submitted solutions.
Identified five prompt structures positioning the LLM mainly as solver, explainer, or validator.
evidence_signal: Ten of the 15 students completing all three tasks changed their dominant prompt structure, while most submissions stayed close to LLM output—even after exchanges involving students’ own explanations, conjectures, and checks.
watch_item: The small, course-specific sample and reliance on chatlog traces limit generalization and may miss thinking outside the recorded exchanges.
paper_title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
